Insights / Research, scanned October 9, 2026

SPECIAL DISTRICT websites and the ADA.

By Noah, founder of Endcap. Published October 11, 2026 · Updated October 25, 2026

The Justice Department’s web accessibility rule gives special districts until April 26, 2028 to make their websites meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA. We scanned the homepages of 38 Orange County special districts and joint powers agencies to see where they stand.

The deadlines

TWO
deadlines.

From ADA.gov. The April 2026 interim final rule extended every compliance date by a year; the technical standard did not change.

April 26, 2027

Larger governments

Cities, counties, and other public entities serving 50,000 people or more.

April 26, 2028

Special districts

Special district governments, and public entities serving fewer than 50,000 people.

Findings

WHAT THE
scan found.

We scanned 38 homepages with axe-core on October 9, 2026.

  1. 01

    32 of the 38 homepages (84%) fail at least one automated WCAG 2.1 check. The median homepage fails 2 kinds of check, on 6 page elements. 10 homepages have at least one failure that axe-core rates critical, such as an image with no text alternative or a button with no name.

  2. 02

    The most common problem is low-contrast text, found on 14 homepages, followed by links with no readable name (13). Both are usually fixed once, in the site’s template.

  3. 03

    23 of the 61 PDFs we checked are untagged or only partly tagged, so screen readers cannot follow their structure all the way through. 15 have no tags at all, and 8 leave some of their pages or text out of the tags. 4 have no text layer at all, which usually means a scanned page, 2 more are scans with readable text on only a few pages, and 20 do not declare a language.

  4. 04

    11 agencies load an accessibility overlay (7 accessiBe, 3 UserWay, 1 AudioEye). 10 of those 11 homepages still fail at least one automated check with the overlay running.

  5. 05

    Automated scans catch only part of what WCAG covers. Keyboard use, reading order, captions, and document structure need a person to check, so a homepage that passes every automated check is not necessarily accessible.

The most common failures

Number of homepages with each failure, of 38.

  1. Text with too little contrastWCAG 1.4.314
  2. Links with no readable nameWCAG 2.4.4, 4.1.213
  3. Button or link names that differ from the visible textWCAG 2.5.39
  4. Images with no text alternativeWCAG 1.1.18
  5. Icons and graphics with no text alternativeWCAG 1.1.17
  6. Buttons with no readable nameWCAG 4.1.24
  7. Form fields with no labelWCAG 4.1.22
  8. Hidden elements that can still take keyboard focusWCAG 4.1.22
  9. Links marked by color aloneWCAG 1.4.12

Before 2028

WHAT TO DO
first.

These six steps are in the order that usually saves the most work.

Ask for a scan
  1. 01

    Scan, then test by hand

    Run an automated scan across the whole site, then check the key pages with a keyboard and a screen reader. Automated tools find only part of the problems.

  2. 02

    Fix the template first

    Contrast, link names, labels, and headings usually live in the theme, so one fix repairs every page that uses it.

  3. 03

    Make new documents accessible

    Agendas, packets, and notices posted from now on should be tagged PDFs or web pages. Older documents can stay as they are only if no one needs them to use a service.

  4. 04

    Set up an archive

    Content kept only for reference can be exempt if it was created before the deadline, sits in a separate archive area, and is not changed.

  5. 05

    Publish a way to ask for help

    Add an accessibility page that gives a contact for anyone who cannot use part of the site, and commit to responding.

  6. 06

    Put it in the contract

    Require WCAG 2.1 Level AA from your website, agenda, and payment vendors, and train the staff who post content.

What is exempt

FIVE
exceptions.

Summarized from ADA.gov. The exceptions do not remove an agency’s duty to provide effective communication or reasonable modifications when someone asks.

Archived content

Content created before the compliance date is exempt if it is kept only for reference, research, or recordkeeping, held in a special archive area, and left unchanged.

Older documents

PDFs, Word files, presentations, and spreadsheets posted before the compliance date are exempt, unless people use them now to apply for or access a service.

Third-party posts

Content posted by members of the public who are not working for the agency is exempt. Content the agency or its vendors post is covered.

Individual documents

Password-protected files about one person, property, or account, such as a bill, are exempt.

Older social media posts

Social media posts made before the compliance date are exempt.

results.

Agencies in the review can ask for their own results: every failure on the homepage, the PDFs we checked, and the fixes that would clear the most problems. We run the same scan for agencies outside the review.

Ask for your results

Method

The agencies are the special districts in OC LAFCO’s directory, plus joint powers agencies, commissions, and the county law library with websites of their own, 41 in total. Each homepage was loaded in Chromium on October 9, 2026 and scanned with axe-core for WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 Level A and AA rules. 3 sites blocked automated visits and are left out, which leaves 38. PDFs are up to eight documents linked from each homepage. 61 from 27 homepages opened, and we checked every page of each for tags and a text layer, and each file for a declared language. 7 links were left out: one file was missing, two links were malformed copies of links we did check, one file was over our 25 MB limit, and three addresses had spaces our checker could not request. Overlay scripts were identified in each homepage’s source on October 10. We publish totals only; no agency is named.

Corrected October 13, 2026. The first version of this page said 18 of the 61 PDFs were untagged and 5 had no text layer. Our checker read a tagged flag set to false as true and looked for text on the first two pages only, so we rechecked the same 61 files page by page on October 12, 2026. The figures above come from that recheck.

Rule details: ADA.gov, Fact Sheet: New Rule on the Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps. This page is a summary, not legal advice.

FAQ

QUESTIONS,
answered.

Anything else? Ask us directly or email Noah at hello@endcap.design.

When do special district websites have to meet the ADA rule?

By April 26, 2028. The Justice Department’s interim final rule of April 20, 2026 moved the date back a year for every group. Public entities serving 50,000 people or more have until April 26, 2027.

What standard does the rule use?

WCAG 2.1 Level AA, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines published by the World Wide Web Consortium. It applies to the agency’s website and mobile apps, including content that vendors provide for it.

Does an accessibility overlay make a website compliant?

An overlay adds a toolbar on top of the page. In our scan, 10 of the 11 homepages with an overlay still failed at least one automated check with the overlay running, so the page itself still needs fixing.

Do old agendas and PDFs need to be fixed?

Documents posted before the compliance date are exempt unless people use them now to apply for or access a service. New agendas, packets, and forms posted after the date are covered.

Which agencies did you scan, and can we see our results?

We scanned the homepages of 38 Orange County agencies: the special districts in OC LAFCO’s directory, plus joint powers agencies, commissions, and the county law library with websites of their own. We do not publish results by agency. An agency can ask for its own results, and we can run the same scan for agencies outside the review.

What does fixing a website usually involve?

Most of the work is in the template: color contrast, link and button names, form labels, and heading structure. Documents are the second part, usually by moving recurring items such as agendas to tagged PDFs or web pages. We quote after looking at the site.
